o1.biggest_strength: The send-window logic: queue step 1 between the 12th and 15th so step 4 lands before month-end close, and route anything that fires during close to the next window. That is a real operator's move, plus it gives reply handling and a compliant footer.
o1.biggest_mistake: Step 1 carries two asks (answer how many days AND reply for a 20-minute walkthrough), which breaks the one-question-one-ask rule, and the 'Bolder move' to blast 300 watch-list contacts with a generic opener undercuts its own recommendation to wait for a trigger.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Make every step one clean ask, drop or reframe the bolder-move section as a controlled A/B test, and tighten the layout so the sequence and list rules are scannable at a glance.

o2.biggest_strength: Honest, reconciled numbers: it plans on ~7%, explicitly refuses to multiply the 6.8% segment rate by the 7.9% trigger gain because the pilot never tested them together, and translates the list into tangible totals (~55 meetings from 1,900). Clean weekly loading cadence and an on-brand 'Close your books faster' subject.
o2.biggest_mistake: Invents a 90-day rest for prior pilot contacts and assumes calendar-day sends/weekend shifts that the brief did not specify; step 1 still leans close to two asks with the 'reply yes' conditional.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Confirm or flag the rest/calendar assumptions more prominently, tighten step 1 to a single ask, and add one extra angle or a quick A/B test plan to widen the range.

reason: Both are genuinely usable and hit the right segment, trigger, link-free step 1 and the 9-to-4 proof, but Output 2 is cleaner, its projections are internally reconciled and honestly hedged, and I could hand it to my team tomorrow with almost no edits.
